prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange sharpened the case more than it altered it. The chair's first question is whether the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and I think it is, for a reason that can be said in one picture. A trapping laser normally shifts the very transition one wants to use as a clock. At the magic wavelength the upper and lower clock levels are shifted by the same amount, so the shift cancels and thousands of atoms can sit in the lattice, free of Doppler and recoil effects, and be interrogated together. The 2005 prize gave us the comb, which counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize gave control of a single trapped quantum system, whose clock uses one ion. The lattice clock is neither of these. It is a new way of holding a large ensemble without disturbing it, and the benefit is statistical as well as systematic: stability that lets one resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, and a clock in which interactions among the atoms became a subject of study in their own right. The evidence that settles the question is empirical. Several laboratories on different continents built Sr and Yb lattice clocks independently, and their intercomparisons agree at the 10^-18 level, so the systematics have been tested by people other than the inventors. Eight of eight members ranked it and all eight proposed the same two names. I do not count that as scientific merit, but it tells me that the attribution is not the weak point, as it is in most of the other candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is the one the chair posed: a third prize in frequency metrology after 2005 and 2012 can be read as a refinement of settled tools, and as an invention with record performance rather than a discovery that tells us something new about nature. Kroll is right that the fundamental-physics payoffs so far, bounds on drifts of constants and on dark-matter couplings, are null results. I accept that this is a real weakness for those who weight a clue from nature most heavily, and it is the reason I keep IceCube and moire graphene as alternatives. Second, the redefinition of the second has not happened. I now agree with Pearce that the citation should not lean on it, since the physics case does not depend on a decision by the General Conference. Third, the ion-clock line (Al+ and others) remains a strong competitor at similar uncertainty, and the practical clock rested on cold-atom engineering and ultrastable lasers developed in many places, so any citation must be worded narrowly. My own bias as an atomic theorist remains, and I discount my enthusiasm for it accordingly.

responses.point: Johansson asks me to state whether early lattice-clock proposals by others affect Katori's priority.
responses.response: I can answer from memory, not from documents in this packet, so I flag it as unverified. Katori proposed trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength around 2001 to 2003 and led the first strontium lattice clock demonstration in 2005 with Takamoto. Earlier proposals existed for optical lattices and for trapped-atom clocks in general, and Pal'chikov, Ovsiannikov and others had calculated light shifts and magic wavelengths in the same years, but I know of nothing that combines the shift-cancelling condition with a complete clock scheme before Katori. So I regard his priority for the concept and the first realization as secure, and the other contributions as the supporting atomic theory, which is the kind of theory work I know well and would not elevate to a prize claim. I would be glad if a colleague with access to the original papers checked the dates, but I do not think the allocation of credit hinges on them.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether Ye's many-body clock work belongs in his credit, and wants a citation that does not imply a single origin for the clock family.
responses.response: I would keep the many-body work as part of the evidence for what the lattice made possible, but not as a separate item in the citation. Ye's role, as I read it, is to have taken the concept to the accuracy and stability frontier, with the 10^-18 level, the millimetre redshift measurement and the spin-exchange and SU(N) physics inside the clock. That is a continuous contribution and the citation wording 'invention and realization' covers it without enumeration. I agree with his qualification that the practical clock needed narrow-line cooling, spin polarization and cavity-stabilized lasers from several laboratories. I disagree only mildly: I would still call the other groups confirmation of the lattice principle, though this does not make them irrelevant to the engineering. The citation should name the principle (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms) and not the clock family at large, which answers his wording concern.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube on a discovery-first principle, says B015 is the safer choice and would test whether lattice clocks are a new principle or an increment.
responses.response: I have tried to give his test a concrete answer above: the magic-wavelength condition is a new principle, and neutral-atom ensembles opened a regime that comb-based and single-ion clocks did not. I do not dismiss his discovery-first view. A diffuse neutrino flux that no model pinned down is exactly what I admire in my own field when something unexpected turns up. My difficulty remains the one he names: three names out of a collaboration of several hundred, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND behind them, and the source evidence still resting largely on two objects. Because I defer to him and Pearce on astroparticle physics, I take his point that the diffuse-flux discovery stands on its own. If the names were settled I would move B007 to a clear second place for this cycle, but I would not put it ahead of the clock today. I read his statement that he would accept B015 as a constructive position and would be glad to hear what citation wording he would need.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that a tunable state-of-matter platform with an explicit theory-to-experiment chain is closer to what condensed-matter prizes have honoured, and that the unresolved pairing mechanism should not disqualify B006.
responses.response: I accept the correction that the existence of the correlated phases is not in doubt, and I now put it less as a defect of the physics and more as a defect of timing and credit. The chain from the Bistritzer-MacDonald model to the 2018 experiments is the cleanest theory-to-experiment story on the list, and I like the simplicity of that model. Where I still differ is that a prize in 2026 would have to name Jarillo-Herrero while Cao, who carried out the experiments, and independent groups sit outside three names, and it would honour a field whose central question, the mechanism of the pairing, is open. I do not hold that against the science, but I judge that the clock has a longer track of independent reproduction. I note that he would not stand in the way of B015, and I keep B006 as my first alternative, so my ranking does not rest on dismissing his candidate.

responses.point: Pearce suggests the citation should rest on the invention and its performance and not on the redefinition of the second, and that reproduction at 1e-18 is the criterion for mature systematics.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my own citation accordingly: it now names the invention, the magic-wavelength mechanism and the 10^-18 performance, with no reference to the redefinition. This also speaks to the chair's question on timing. If the redefinition slips, the physics case is unaffected, and if it comes it will confirm that the community already trusts these clocks. I would treat it as supporting evidence of timeliness, not a condition. I also share his view that a two-part configuration is not preferable here, since the partners suggested so far (IceCube and atom interferometry) carry credit problems that would weaken a prize that is otherwise clean.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the flat-band mechanism in B006 is understood and not only observed, and that a prize would honour that and not a theory of superconductivity.
responses.response: That is a fair framing and it tempers my earlier worry about the open mechanism. I agree that the clock is also understood at depth, since the systematic shifts are modelled and cross-checked across laboratories, but I accept that it is a measurement achievement and not a new mechanism of the type he values. We differ in what we put first and I do not think we can settle this by argument. My remaining concern is practical: with Cao and the independent groups outside the three names, the committee would be choosing among experimental credits that I find harder to defend today than the two-name clock attribution.

uncertainties: Priority details among early magic-wavelength and lattice-clock proposals are recalled from memory and not verified against the original papers.
Whether the committee will treat the clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which I think it is, but which is a judgement and not a measurement.
Whether a citation naming magic-wavelength trapping and 'invention and realization' divides credit between Katori and Ye in a way that colleagues find fair.
The maturity and attribution of B006 and B007, on which I rely mostly on colleagues with direct expertise.
How the ion-clock line and the timing of the redefinition of the second will develop, which might change the relative weight of the prize in later years.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller (ETH) attosecond groups, but I have no apparent connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, and none to the candidates in B006 or B007. Atomic physics is my own field, which is a bias to declare and not a recusal ground. Having read the round-1 statements, I see no new conflicts.
